strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized to distributed self-routing, addressing genuine limitations (inflexibility, capability-assessment bottleneck) of existing router-based systems.
Clean and rigorous problem formulation (Section 2) that clearly contrasts centralized vs. distributed optimization objectives.

Comprehensive experimental suite: multiple scenarios (performance/balance/cost-first), in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, modularity/flexibility tests (3-agent reduced pool), and comparison to a reasonably broad set of routing baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter).

Thoughtful diagnostic analyses: system- and agent-level scenario adaptability plots, easy/hard query cost differentiation, comparison of intrinsic self-assessment vs. external classifiers (Table 5), and a useful control experiment (Appendix J) confirming that gains stem from self-awareness rather than raw task-performance improvement from training.
Reward rationality analysis (Section 3.2.3) provides a clean theoretical justification for the reject-reward design and its scenario-dependent threshold behavior.
Good reproducibility documentation of training hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset statistics in the appendix.
weaknesses: The LLM pool used throughout is a single homogeneous model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct at different sizes), which substantially weakens the central claim of a 'distributed network of heterogeneous LLM agents'; the setting is closer to a self-aware cascade of same-family checkpoints than a realistic multi-vendor/multi-architecture agent network.

Despite claiming generality to tree/mesh topologies in the discussion, all experiments use only the simplest cascade structure; the more interesting distributed-network claims are unvalidated speculation deferred to future work.

The reward function design (rejection threshold = 1-α in SFT, reward = (1-α)^γ in RL, with γ=0.5) appears somewhat ad hoc; no ablation over γ or alternative functional forms is provided to justify this specific choice beyond a qualitative argument.

In Table 2, DiSRouter's raw accuracy is often lower than several baselines (e.g., Automix, Largest LLM) in the Performance-First setting; the utility advantage largely stems from lower cost, and it is unclear whether the utility metric or scenario/threshold design inherently favors DiSRouter's construction.
No statistical significance testing, variance, or multiple-seed reporting is provided for the main results, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported utility gains.

Baseline implementations for FrugalGPT/FORC substitute DistilBERT with a larger Qwen2.5-0.5B model 'due to poor performance,' which could bias comparisons in DiSRouter's favor and is not fully justified.

The core techniques (rejection-based training, self-awareness alignment) build closely on prior work (Xu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025); the main novelty is largely the system-level framing and reward conditioning on α rather than a fundamentally new training method.

The action space restricting an agent to only route to higher-cost agents (Eq. 4) simplifies the true distributed routing problem considerably, and the fallback to the largest model as 'expert of last resort' is not analyzed for failure cases (e.g., when the largest model is also overconfident/wrong).

strengths: The paper is clearly written with good figures (Fig. 1-2) that effectively communicate the centralized vs. distributed routing concept and the training pipeline.

The core idea of using intrinsic LLM self-awareness (reject/answer) instead of an external router classifier is intuitive and is supported by a reasonably convincing probe (Table 5) showing the aligned model's rejection decision outperforms external BERT- and LLM-based classifiers at predicting solvability.

The scenario-conditioned reward with the (1-alpha)^gamma rejection reward is a simple, interpretable mechanism, and the authors provide a short theoretical rationale (Sec 3.2.3) for why it induces the desired threshold behavior.

Reasonably thorough experimental analysis including in-domain, out-of-domain generalization, modularity/plug-and-play ablation, and system/agent-level behavior analysis (Figs 4-7) that attempts to explain why the method works, not just that it works.
Appendix J thoughtfully isolates whether gains come from improved task capability vs. improved self-awareness, which strengthens the core claim.
weaknesses: The entire empirical validation is restricted to a single homogeneous model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct at 5 sizes). The paper's motivation explicitly centers on a 'diverse ecosystem' of heterogeneous LLMs from different vendors/families with non-monotonic capability profiles, yet no experiment uses heterogeneous models. This substantially undercuts the central claims about flexibility, modularity, and superiority over external routers in realistic, heterogeneous routing settings.

The routing topology is restricted to a simple monotonic cascade where an agent can only forward to strictly higher-cost agents (Eq. 4). The more general topologies (tree, mesh) that are used to motivate 'distributed routing' as a paradigm shift are only discussed qualitatively in the Discussion section and never implemented or evaluated, so the paper's main architectural novelty claim is largely unvalidated.

The 'modularity' experiment (Table 4) only removes two models from the same homogeneous cascade (reducing 5 to 3 agents) rather than testing addition of a genuinely new/different LLM, which was the concrete inflexibility problem described in the introduction (Fig. 1, 'New LLM'). This is a much weaker test than what the paper's motivating example promises.

Several baselines (FrugalGPT, FORC) were modified by replacing their originally specified scorer (DistilBERT) with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct 'because we observed poor performance,' which is an ad hoc, under-justified change that could bias comparisons in the authors' favor or make reproducibility/fairness questionable.

RouteLLM's reported accuracy (e.g., 0.44 in Table 2) is lower than even the Random baseline (0.67), which is suspicious and suggests a possible implementation/adaptation issue (RouteLLM was designed for binary strong/weak routing, not K-way), undermining confidence in the baseline comparisons used to claim DiSRouter's superiority.

Cost is operationalized purely as GPU inference time within one cluster/model family rather than realistic heterogeneous costs (e.g., API pricing across providers), which weakens the practical relevance of the utility metric to the motivating 'diverse ecosystem' scenario with real cost heterogeneity.

The core training technique (reject-based reliability training via SFT+RL) closely follows prior work (Xu et al. 2024) on refusal training; the main addition is a scenario-conditioned reward and applying it independently across a size cascade, which is an incremental rather than fundamentally novel contribution.

Key design choices such as gamma=0.5 in the reward function are set without systematic ablation or sensitivity analysis, and RL sometimes reduces accuracy relative to SFT alone (e.g., Performance First: 0.84 -> 0.81) without a thorough discussion of when/why this trade-off is beneficial.

No real-world or human evaluation, and no experiments at larger model scale or with reasoning-heavy state-of-the-art LLMs, limiting evidence that findings will hold in practical deployment settings beyond the controlled, same-family benchmark used here.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized to distributed self-routing, with a rigorous problem formulation (Section 2) that cleanly contrasts centralized vs. distributed objectives.

The two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT + scenario-conditioned RL) is a sensible and technically grounded contribution, including a theoretical reward-rationality analysis (Eq. 8-10) explaining why the chosen reward form yields the desired threshold behavior.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 7 in-domain and 3 out-of-domain datasets, three cost/performance scenarios, and multiple analyses (scenario adaptability at system/agent level, easy/hard query discrimination, self-awareness vs. external classifiers, modularity with a reduced 3-agent pool).

Thoughtful ablation isolating whether gains come from improved self-awareness vs. improved raw task performance (Appendix J), strengthening the causal claim that self-awareness, not capability gain, drives utility improvements.
Reasonably strong and honest reproducibility/implementation documentation (training hyperparameters, prompts, dataset splits, baseline reimplementation details).
weaknesses: The LLM pool is homogeneous (five sizes of the same Qwen2.5 family), which does not reflect the heterogeneous, multi-vendor ecosystem motivating the paper (e.g., GPT-5-style unified routing across very different model families/architectures); results may not generalize to truly diverse model pools with different training data/biases.

Each agent must undergo the proposed SFT+RL self-awareness training before being added to the cascade, which undercuts the claimed 'plug-and-play' flexibility and modularity: a new or proprietary/API-only LLM cannot simply be inserted without this (non-trivial) alignment procedure, and the 'modularity' experiment only removes existing pre-trained agents rather than adding a genuinely new, untrained one.

Baselines such as FrugalGPT and FORC were modified by replacing their original small scoring models (DistilBERT) with a larger Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct due to 'poor performance,' which could make comparisons less faithful to the original methods and potentially advantage/disadvantage certain baselines inconsistently.

Only the simple cascade topology is actually evaluated; the tree/mesh architectures advertised as a core flexibility advantage of the distributed paradigm remain purely discussed/future work, so the claimed generality of the framework is not empirically validated.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs (single-seed numbers in all tables), and the utility gap to the Oracle topline remains substantial (DiSRouter reaches only ~74-85% of Oracle utility), suggesting room for stronger claims of near-optimality.

The evaluation is restricted to short-form QA/classification-style benchmarks with binary correctness; it is unclear how self-awareness training and the reject mechanism would transfer to open-ended generation tasks where correctness is not binary.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized to distributed self-routing, addressing genuine limitations (inflexibility, limited capability of external routers) of prior work.

Very extensive experimental evaluation: main results across three scenarios, out-of-domain generalization, modularity/flexibility tests (3-agent reduced system), scenario adaptability analysis at both system and agent level, comparison of intrinsic self-assessment vs external classifiers, and a careful ablation confirming that gains come from self-awareness rather than raw capability improvement (Pass@10 analysis).

Thoughtful reward design (percentile/threshold-based scenario-conditioned reward with a reliability exponent γ) accompanied by a clear theoretical rationality analysis explaining the resulting decision threshold behavior.

Good breadth of supplementary studies in the appendix: heterogeneous model families (Gemma-3, Phi-4), closed-source GPT-series intrinsic self-awareness experiments, open-ended generative tasks (summarization) with continuous reward adaptation, and time-overhead/latency analysis showing routing cost is negligible.
Reasonably strong reproducibility statement with detailed training/implementation hyperparameters and dataset descriptions provided.
weaknesses: The routing topology is restricted to a simple cascade with strictly increasing cost order; while the authors acknowledge this and discuss more general topologies as future work, the core empirical claims of 'distributed routing with arbitrary structure' are not actually tested beyond this simplified case.

Despite claims of superior flexibility over centralized routers, each new/updated LLM in the pool still requires its own dedicated SFT+RL self-awareness training, which is nontrivial compute and partially undercuts the 'plug-and-play' framing (though admittedly better than full-system retraining).

The utility gains over the strongest baseline (GraphRouter) are often modest (e.g., 0.73 vs 0.68, 0.61 vs 0.53, 0.52 vs 0.45 in Table 2), and DiSRouter still reaches only ~74-80% of Oracle utility, leaving a substantial gap to the theoretical optimum.

RL training sometimes reduces raw accuracy relative to SFT (e.g., 0.84→0.81, 0.83→0.77, 0.77→0.75 in Table 2) while improving utility mainly through reduced cost; this raises the question of whether RL is teaching better 'self-awareness' or simply learning to reject more aggressively (a form of reward shaping) rather than genuinely refined capability boundary estimation.

The self-awareness training data construction (rejecting based on sampled correctness frequency) risks conflating 'difficulty as measured by this specific model's stochastic outputs' with genuine epistemic self-knowledge, and this could partly explain the good separation results in Section 4.3 as an artifact of the training signal rather than independent evidence of 'intrinsic' self-awareness.

Main experiments are restricted to a single homogeneous model family (Qwen2.5); the more externally interesting heterogeneous-family and closed-source-model experiments are relegated to the appendix with fewer baselines and less thorough analysis.
No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for the main results, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported utility differences.

Some baseline implementations (e.g., RouteLLM achieving only 0.44 accuracy under Performance-First despite being designed to route to the smallest capable model) seem unusually weak, raising questions about whether all baselines were tuned to comparable rigor as the proposed method.

The paper's core mechanism (LLM cascades with confidence-based rejection) is conceptually close to prior self-verification/refusal-based cascade work (e.g., AutoMix, Xu et al. 2024 rejection training); the primary novelty is combining this with an RL scenario-conditioned reward, which is a solid but somewhat incremental technical contribution rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (LLM routing) and proposes a conceptually clean alternative to centralized routers by using distributed, self-assessing agents, which is an interesting reframing of the routing problem.

The two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT + RL with a localized, scenario-conditioned reward) is a reasonably well-engineered mechanism to induce calibrated rejection behavior, and the reward rationality analysis (threshold derivation, gamma discussion) is a nice touch.

Extensive appendix experiments cover many angles: time/latency overhead, out-of-domain generalization, modularity with reduced agent pools, different model families (Gemma, Phi), open-ended generative tasks, and intrinsic self-awareness of closed-source GPT models, showing an attempt at thorough empirical validation.

The system-level and agent-level analyses (routing distribution shift, answer-rate changes with alpha, accuracy gap between answered/rejected subsets) provide reasonably convincing mechanistic evidence for why the method works, beyond just aggregate utility numbers.
Scenario adaptability via a single unified model (rather than retraining per alpha as GraphRouter requires) is a genuine practical advantage if it holds up under more rigorous testing.
weaknesses: The core architecture is restricted to a strictly ordered cascade of homogeneous models of increasing size/cost; the claimed generality to tree/mesh topologies is only discussed speculatively in Section 6 and never implemented or evaluated, so the 'distributed routing network' framing is considerably oversold relative to what is actually tested.

The method fundamentally relies on each agent producing a binary accept/reject decision, which is a much coarser action space than what full external routers (e.g., GraphRouter) use (ranking among K models); this simplification may unfairly advantage DiSRouter's framing and makes the comparison to baselines somewhat apples-to-oranges, since baselines must solve a harder K-way assignment problem.

The RL reward (Eq. 7) gives 0 reward to incorrect answers but allows reward (1-alpha)^gamma for rejection even when the model could have answered correctly; this encourages excessive conservatism and the chosen gamma=0.5 is justified only by an informal plot/argument (Figure 3) rather than ablation over gamma showing sensitivity or robustness of final utility.

Utility gains over baselines, while consistent, are often modest and sometimes dataset/scenario-dependent (e.g., Table 2 Performance-First: DiSRouter+RL utility 0.73 vs. GraphRouter 0.68; Cost-First: 0.52 vs 0.45), and the system reaches only ~74-80% of Oracle utility, leaving open whether the architectural novelty translates into a clearly superior practical system versus simpler cascading heuristics (e.g., FrugalGPT reaches 0.64 utility in Performance-First with much simpler design).

All main experiments use a single homogeneous model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct) of 5 sizes with strictly increasing cost assigned heuristically (not real-world API pricing), and the datasets are mostly simple multiple-choice/QA benchmarks; the heterogeneous/family generalization and GPT-series experiments are relegated to the appendix with much weaker baseline coverage (only 3 baselines), undercutting confidence that results generalize to realistic, more diverse, or more complex task settings.

The RL training is described as being done 'completely independently and in parallel' per agent, but it's unclear how the training data/distribution for an agent (especially mid-cascade agents) accounts for the fact that in deployment they only see queries that were rejected by upstream agents, not the full query distribution used for training -- this potential train/test distribution mismatch is not discussed or ablated.

Baseline implementations substitute the originally proposed scoring models (e.g., DistilBERT in FrugalGPT/FORC) with 'better performing' Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct variants chosen by the authors, which could bias comparisons in unclear directions and reduces faithfulness/reproducibility of baseline results relative to their original papers.

The claim that 'DiSRouter's performance gains do not stem from a direct improvement in task performance due to training' (Section 4.3, backed by Pass@10 deltas <1%) is based on a fairly coarse metric and limited analysis; it doesn't fully rule out more subtle shifts in calibration or confidence that could conflate self-awareness gains with capability changes.

The paper's core 'External Router vs Intrinsic Assessment' comparison (Table 5) trains external classifiers on a fixed 7B model's correctness labels using limited data/architectures (BERT-base, 8B LLM) without extensive hyperparameter tuning details, and the conclusion that intrinsic self-assessment is inherently superior rests on this single comparison rather than a broader sweep of external-router designs or sizes.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean paradigm shift from centralized external routers to distributed self-routing, addressing well-motivated limitations (inflexibility to pool changes, inaccurate capability assessment by small external routers).

Proposes a principled two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT + RL) with a theoretically justified scenario-conditioned reward (including a rationality analysis of the reward's threshold behavior), enabling fully independent/parallel training of agents and tunable performance-cost tradeoffs via a single preference factor.

Extensive main and appendix experiments: in-domain and OOD evaluation across 10 datasets, modularity test with a reduced 3-agent pool, generalization to heterogeneous model families (Gemma-3, Phi-4), extension to open-ended generative tasks (summarization with BERTScore-based reward), and experiments probing intrinsic self-awareness in both open- and closed-source LLMs (GPT-4.1 series, o4-mini).

Strong supporting analyses that directly interrogate the claimed mechanism: comparison of intrinsic self-assessment vs. trained external classifiers (BERT- and LLM-based) showing superior discriminative accuracy/F1, analysis showing accuracy gap between answered/rejected subsets, and an explicit check (Pass@10) confirming utility gains come from improved self-awareness rather than incidental task-capability improvement.

Practical considerations are addressed carefully, including a detailed time/latency overhead analysis showing routing cost is negligible relative to inference cost and favorable compared to cascading/self-verification baselines like FrugalGPT and AutoMix.
Good reproducibility: datasets, models, training hyperparameters, and prompts are all specified in detail, and the method relies on open-source backbones and public benchmarks.
weaknesses: The core architecture evaluated is a simple linear cascade with strictly increasing-cost routing; more complex topologies (tree, mesh) that the paper claims the paradigm generalizes to are only discussed conceptually in Section 6 and not empirically validated.

The claimed 'plug-and-play' modularity is somewhat overstated: while removing agents is training-free, truly adding a new heterogeneous agent to the system still requires running the full Self-Awareness SFT+RL pipeline on it before it can reliably self-assess, which is a nontrivial training cost compared to the instantaneous updates implied by the framing.

DiSRouter still falls meaningfully short of the Oracle topline (e.g., ~74-80% of oracle utility in main results), and the gap is not deeply analyzed—it's unclear whether this stems from imperfect self-awareness, cascading error accumulation, or the strict monotonic-cost routing constraint.

Main experiments use a single homogeneous model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct) across only 5 sizes up to 14B; the more convincing heterogeneous/model-family and closed-source experiments are relegated to the appendix with less rigorous baseline comparisons (e.g., fewer baselines, single scenario in Table 18/20 contexts).

Some hyperparameters (e.g., γ=0.5 reliability factor, SFT thresholding via δ=1-α) are chosen heuristically/by designer preference rather than tuned or justified empirically across a range, raising questions about sensitivity and robustness.

Baseline implementations substitute different backbone scorers (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct instead of DistilBERT for FrugalGPT/FORC) due to reported poor performance of the original setups, which could affect the fairness of the comparison against DiSRouter, which benefits from substantial additional training (SFT+RL) not afforded equally to baselines.

The method fundamentally depends on binary/scalar correctness signals for SFT data construction; the extension to open-ended tasks requires a reliable external reward model (e.g., BERTScore), which reintroduces a form of external assessment dependency that is not deeply discussed as a limitation.
